card: Why homeowners go quiet after a quote, the three message follow up that gets replies, and how to stop handing your drawings to a cheaper competitor.
title: Customer Ghosted After a Quote? The Follow Up That Works
desc: Customer ghosted you after a quote? Why homeowners go quiet, a three message follow up text that gets replies, and how to stop wasting hours quoting.

blocks.h1: Ghosted after a quote? *Here is what to send.*
blocks.lede: Most homeowners who go quiet after a quote are not being rude. They got several quotes, someone was cheaper or quicker, and saying no feels awkward, so they say nothing. You cannot stop it completely, but a ballpark price first, an expiry date on every quote and a short follow up sequence win back a surprising share.
ticks: A three message follow up you can copy
How to protect hours of quoting work

blocks.html:
Why do customers ghost after a quote?

Contractors on Reddit put the number anywhere from one in five to well over half. Homeowners explain it from the other side in the same threads:

  • They got several quotes and went with someone else, usually cheaper or faster.
  • Saying no feels awkward. Some worry about an angry reply, so silence feels safer.
  • The price shocked them and they need time, or the project is now on hold.
  • Life got in the way. The quote sits in an inbox under fifty other emails.

Only the last two are winnable, but they are more common than most trades think.

Stop it before the quote: three habits

  1. Give a ballpark first. On the first call, give a rough range. People who cannot afford it drop out before you spend six hours measuring and pricing.
  2. Put an expiry date on every quote. Seven to fourteen days is common. It gives you a natural reason to follow up and nudges people to decide.
  3. Keep the valuable parts until there is a deposit. Trades repeatedly report homeowners taking detailed drawings and specs to a cheaper builder. Quote the job; hand over the design work once they commit.

The follow up sequence that gets replies

Short, friendly and easy to answer. Send by text if that is how they first contacted you.

Day 2: “Hi Sam, just checking the quote for your driveway came through okay. Happy to walk you through any of it. Cheers, Jake.”

Day 6: “Hi Sam, a quick heads up: the price on your quote is held until Friday. If the timing or budget has changed, just let me know and I can look at options.”

Day 12: “Hi Sam, I will close this one off on my side so I am not chasing you. If you go ahead with someone else, no hard feelings at all, and if anything changes I am happy to help.”

The last message works because it makes saying no easy. A lot of people reply to it, and some of those replies are “sorry, still keen, can we start next month?”

Call, do not just email

A two minute phone call on day two or three wins more work than any email. You learn whether price, timing or trust is the problem, and you can often fix it on the spot with a smaller scope, a payment plan or a later start date.

Make your quote the easy choice

When a homeowner compares three quotes, they also compare the businesses. The trade with recent Google reviews, photos of similar jobs and a clear website looks like the safer bet even at a higher price. That is the quiet reason some trades get ghosted less: the homeowner checked them out and felt sure. See what a trade website needs to win that comparison.

How to write a quote that wins more often

  • Lead with the outcome, not the materials list: “New 60 square metre exposed aggregate driveway, ready to drive on in 7 days.”
  • Spell out what is included and what is not, so cheaper quotes that leave things out look worse next to yours.
  • Offer options. A good, better and best version lets people choose a level instead of choosing a competitor.
  • Add proof: two or three photos of similar jobs and a short review.
  • Show the timeline and the payment stages, so there are no surprises.
  • Make it easy to say yes: a clear next step, a deposit link, a date you can start.

When you lose the job anyway

Ask, kindly: “No problem at all. Would you mind telling me what made the difference? It helps me improve.” Most people will answer. If price keeps coming up, you may be quoting the wrong customers; if trust keeps coming up, your reviews and online presence need work. Either way you learn more from one honest answer than from ten silent ones.

blocks.title: Your checklist.
items: Give a rough price range on the first call
Add a 7 to 14 day expiry date to every quote
Keep drawings and detailed designs until a deposit is paid
Follow up by text on day 2
Send a price held reminder around day 6
Close it off politely around day 12
Track how many quotes you win and lose

items.q: How long should I wait to follow up on a quote?
items.a: Two days is a good first follow up. Most trades send two or three messages over about two weeks, then close it off politely.

items.q: Should a quote have an expiry date?
items.a: Yes. Seven to fourteen days is common. It protects you from material price rises and gives the customer a reason to decide.

items.q: Is it rude to follow up on a quote?
items.a: No. Most homeowners expect it, and many are glad of the reminder. Keep it short and make it easy for them to say no.

items.q: How do I stop people using my drawings with another builder?
items.a: Quote the job without handing over detailed drawings or designs, and charge a design fee or take a deposit before you release them.

items.q: Why do I lose quotes to cheaper contractors?
items.a: Often because the homeowner cannot see the difference. Reviews, photos of similar work and a clear explanation of what is included help justify a higher price.
